description.en: Reasoning models in 2026 don't just answer once — they sample the problem several times and let the answers vote. Self-consistency decoding is the simplest form of test-time compute: same question, many independent tries, majority wins.

story_variants.en:
## One Guess Is Risky. Five Guesses That Vote Isn't.

"Ask a reasoning model a hard question once, and one unlucky reasoning path can derail the whole answer," Vaathiyaar says. "So instead of trusting a single greedy pass, 2026's reasoning models spend extra **test-time compute**: sample the same question several times, at some temperature, each run reasoning independently — then let the final answers **vote**."

### Self-Consistency Decoding

This technique is called **self-consistency**: run the model N times on the same prompt, extract each run's final answer, and keep whichever answer appears most often. Wrong reasoning paths tend to scatter across different wrong answers; the *correct* path tends to get reached multiple independent ways, so it usually wins the vote even when no single sample is trustworthy alone.

```
sample 1 -> "42"
sample 2 -> "41"
sample 3 -> "42"
sample 4 -> "42"
sample 5 -> "40"

majority vote -> "42"   (3 out of 5 samples agree)
```

### Why This Counts As "Test-Time Compute"

Nothing about the model's weights changed. All the extra accuracy came from spending more **inference-time compute** — more sampled reasoning chains — on the same fixed model. This is the core idea behind the 2026 shift from "bigger models" to "more thoughtful models": inference compute, not just parameter count, has become a lever for accuracy.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if one sample might be wrong, ask again — several times — and count. Self-consistency turns raw sampling noise into a confidence signal.

Today you implement the vote itself: which answer wins, and how confident was the crowd?

q.en: Why is self-consistency called a form of "test-time compute"?
q.ta: Self-consistency ஏன் "test-time compute" இன் ஒரு வடிவம் என்று அழைக்கப்படுகிறது?

en: It switches to a model with more parameters at test time
It retrains the model's weights on each new question
It runs only one greedy pass to save compute
It spends more inference compute sampling a fixed model
ta: test நேரத்தில் அதிக parameters கொண்ட மாடலுக்கு மாறுகிறது
ஒவ்வொரு புதிய கேள்விக்கும் மாடலின் weights-ஐ மீண்டும் பயிற்றுவிக்கிறது
compute-ஐ மிச்சப்படுத்த ஒரே ஒரு greedy pass மட்டும் இயக்குகிறது
மாறாத ஒரே மாடலில் பல முறை sample செய்ய அதிக inference compute செலவிடுகிறது

q.en: Why does the correct answer usually win the vote, even when no single sample is trustworthy?
q.ta: எந்த ஒரு sample-உம் நம்பகமானதாக இல்லாவிட்டாலும், சரியான பதில் பொதுவாக ஏன் வாக்கெடுப்பில் வெல்கிறது?

en: The model always gives the right answer at high temperature
Wrong answers are deleted before the vote is counted
Later samples are weighted more heavily than early ones
Wrong paths scatter; the right answer is reached many ways

uth_example:
from collections import Counter

question = "A shop sells pens at 3 for 10. How much for 12 pens?"
reasoning_paths = [
    ("12 / 3 = 4 packs, 4 * 10", "40"),
    ("each pen 3.33, 12 * 3.33", "39.96"),
    ("4 packs of 3, 4 * 10", "40"),
    ("12 * 10 / 3", "40"),
    ("3 + 10 = 13 per pen?", "156"),
]

answers = [ans for _, ans in reasoning_paths]
counts = Counter(answers)
winner, votes = counts.most_common(1)[0]
confidence = votes / len(answers)
print(counts)
print(f"answer {winner} with {confidence:.0%} agreement")
